title: World War I
summary: World War I (1914–1918) was a global conflict between the Allied and Central Powers that mobilised over 65 million soldiers. Triggered by the Sarajevo assassination, it introduced industrialised trench warfare, destroyed four empires, and left an estimated 16 million soldiers and civilians dead.
card: Between 1914 and 1918, the Allied Powers defeated the Central Powers in a global war fought across European trenches, the Middle East, Africa, and world sea lanes. The conflict cost more than 8.5 million military lives and millions of civilian deaths through combat, blockades, and genocidal deportations. Its aftermath toppled the German, Austro-Hungarian, Russian, and Ottoman dynasties, transforming international boundaries and generating political instability that presaged the Second World War.
what:
World War I, initially known as the Great War, was an international conflict that pitted the Allied Powers—chiefly Great Britain, France, the Russian Empire, Italy, Japan, and later the United States—against the Central Powers of Germany, Austria-Hungary, the Ottoman Empire, and Bulgaria. The conflict began in the Balkans following the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand in Sarajevo on 28 June 1914 and widened into general war across Europe by early August 1914.

Fighting occurred across multiple continents and oceans, but the conflict was defined above all by the Western Front, where opposing armies built an elaborate system of trenches stretching over 600 kilometres from the North Sea to the Swiss border. The Eastern Front witnessed vast movements of troops across Poland and Russia, while additional theatres developed in the Alpine mountains of Italy, the Gallipoli peninsula, Mesopotamia, Palestine, and East Africa. Technological innovations transformed combat through machine guns, long-range heavy artillery, poison gas, flamethrowers, tanks, combat aircraft, and submarines.

The human toll was unprecedented in modern history. More than 8.5 million soldiers died in military service, and combat wounded reached an estimated 21 million. Civilian mortality was likewise severe, with historians estimating that as many as 13 million non-combatants perished from starvation, military violence, infectious disease, and state-sponsored massacres, including the Ottoman deportations of Armenians. Disagreement persists among demographic historians over exact civilian totals because wartime blockades, famine, and the concurrent 1918 influenza pandemic produced overlapping causes of death that civil registrations could not fully distinguish.

The war concluded in late 1918 after an Allied counter-offensive broke German resistance on the Western Front. Following the abdication of Emperor Wilhelm II, an armistice took effect on 11 November 1918. The formal peace terms were dictated by the victorious powers at the Paris Peace Conference, culminating in the Treaty of Versailles signed on 28 June 1919.

uncertainty.note: Hostilities commenced with Austria-Hungary's declaration of war on Serbia on 28 July 1914 following the Sarajevo assassination of 28 June 1914; combat on the Western Front ended with the Armistice of 11 November 1918, while the formal legal state of war concluded with the Treaty of Versailles on 28 June 1919 and subsequent treaties.

how:
The immediate trigger of the war was the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand of Austria in Sarajevo on 28 June 1914 by Gavrilo Princip, a member of the Young Bosnia nationalist movement. During the ensuing July Crisis, Austria-Hungary secured unconditional German backing and delivered an ultimatum to Serbia, declaring war on 28 July 1914. This action set off a chain reaction among interlocking European alliances: Russia mobilized to protect Serbia; Germany declared war on Russia and France, launching the Schlieffen Plan through neutral Belgium; and Great Britain entered the war in defense of Belgian neutrality on 4 August 1914.

The initial German drive toward Paris was halted at the Battle of the Marne in September 1914, after which both sides dug extensive trench systems, establishing a defensive stalemate on the Western Front. On the Eastern Front, German forces under Paul von Hindenburg smashed Russian armies at Tannenberg, opening a fluid campaign of deep advances. The Ottoman Empire entered on the German side in late 1914, prompting the British and French to mount the Gallipoli amphibious landings in 1915, which failed with heavy casualties. In Africa, British and South African forces waged a protracted four-year campaign against German askari forces under Paul von Lettow-Vorbeck.

The conflict evolved into total war, requiring national economic mobilization, conscription, and the extensive recruitment of colonial troops, including 1.5 million Indian Army soldiers and hundreds of thousands of African carriers and combatants. In 1916, massive attritional offensives at Verdun and the Somme produced hundreds of thousands of casualties without decisive strategic breakthroughs. The strategic balance shifted in 1917: Germany's resumption of unrestricted submarine warfare brought the United States into the war on 6 April 1917, while revolutionary upheaval in Russia led the Bolshevik government to exit the conflict via the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk in March 1918. A final German Spring Offensive in 1918 exhausted Germany's armies, allowing Allied and American forces under Marshal Ferdinand Foch to launch the Hundred Days Offensive. Facing domestic revolution and military collapse, German representatives signed an armistice in a railway carriage at Compiègne, ending combat on 11 November 1918.
why_it_matters:
World War I dismantled the imperial architecture of nineteenth-century Europe, bringing about the downfall of four ruling dynasties: the Romanovs in Russia, the Hohenzollerns in Germany, the Habsburgs in Austria-Hungary, and the Ottomans in the Middle East. From their ruins emerged new nation-states across Central and Eastern Europe, including Poland, Czechoslovakia, and Yugoslavia, while the Paris Peace Conference established the League of Nations as the world's first permanent collective security organisation. However, the punitive financial reparations and territorial transfers imposed by the Treaty of Versailles, combined with economic devastation and political radicalization, created profound grievances in Germany and Italy that facilitated the rise of totalitarian fascist movements. In the colonized world, the wartime service and sacrifices of millions of Asian and African troops fostered new political consciousness and sharpened demands for self-determination, directly accelerating anti-colonial independence campaigns in India and Africa.

The war also inaugurated the era of modern industrialized warfare, transforming military doctrine and leaving enduring institutional legacies in international humanitarian law. Without the initial German operational failure at the Marne in September 1914, Paris might have fallen within weeks, potentially averting four years of catastrophic trench stalemate. Had the United States maintained strict neutrality rather than committing two million troops and crucial financial resources in 1917–1918, the exhausted European combatants could have been forced into an inconclusive negotiated peace rather than total German collapse. The unresolved territorial rivalries and ideological hatreds forged in the trenches directly generated the geopolitical crisis that produced the Second World War twenty years later.

related.title: Assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand
related.because: The fatal shooting of the Austro-Hungarian heir by Gavrilo Princip in Sarajevo triggered the diplomatic July Crisis and the mobilization of opposing alliances.
Catastrophic military casualties, acute food shortages, and financial exhaustion produced by the war triggered the overthrow of the Russian imperial autocracy and the Bolshevik revolution.

The destabilization of Central Europe, punitive reparations, and intense revanchist nationalism arising from the Versailles settlement and the war guilt clause directly enabled the conditions for the outbreak of World War II.

Prolonged attritional battles at Verdun and the Somme inflict massive casualties, including over 57,000 British casualties on 1 July 1916 alone.

perspectives.holder: Fritz Fischer (1961), Griff nach der Weltmacht and orthodox German-war-guilt school
perspectives.account: Imperial Germany deliberately exploited the July Crisis following the Sarajevo assassination, issuing a blank cheque to Austria-Hungary in a premeditated attempt to achieve continental hegemony and break encirclement before Russian military reforms matured, thus bearing primary culpability for triggering general European war.

perspectives.holder: Christopher Clark (2012), The Sleepwalkers, and revisionist multi-polar school
perspectives.account: World War I resulted not from a single state's deliberate master plan, but from a tragedy of collective miscalculation, mutual paranoia, military mobilization timetables, and brittle alliance mechanisms in which European leaders acted as sleepwalkers unaware of the catastrophe they were provoking.

perspectives.holder: C. Paul Vincent (1985) and economic historians on the Allied naval blockade
perspectives.account: The Allied naval blockade of Germany was a catastrophic instrument of economic attrition that denied food and raw materials to the civilian population, causing an estimated 400,000 to 700,000 excess civilian deaths and critically shattering the German home front by late 1918.

audience_note: Contains descriptions and historical documentation of industrialised warfare, poison gas casualties, trench fighting, wartime famine, and mass atrocities against civilians, including the Armenian genocide.

importance.justification: Global conflict that mobilized over 65 million men, brought about the collapse of four continental empires, cost an estimated 16 million lives, and reshaped modern international borders and political systems.

reviewer_note: Coordinator review: WWI civilian and total death ranges trimmed to what the cited pages state (as many as 13 million civilians; an estimated 16 million total). Least sure of the exact global tally of civilian deaths (estimates run as high as 13 million owing to unrecorded war-related famine and disease, compounded by the 1918 influenza outbreak) and whether the official termination of the war should be anchored to the 11 November 1918 Armistice or the 28 June 1919 Treaty of Versailles.
